cim: Artificial Intelligence, Critical Minerals, and the Financial Abandonment of American Manufacturing
cim_eredeti: Artificial Intelligence, Critical Minerals, and the Financial Abandonment of American Manufacturing
szoveg_eredeti:
Why can American financial markets mobilize hundreds of billions of dollars annually for artificial intelligence, a technology whose ultimate profitability remains uncertain, while struggling to finance the reconstruction of industrial capabilities whose necessity is already clear?

I believe that this question goes to the heart of America’s critical minerals crisis. It also exposes a fundamental weakness in the financial system that has come to dominate American industrial policy, corporate management, and capital allocation.

Wall Street has discovered artificial intelligence, and the capital being committed to its development is extraordinary. Reuters reported on October 7, 2026, that the world’s largest technology companies’ combined capital spending plans had risen to more than $730 billion for the year. In June, Morgan Stanley projected that global AI-related debt issuance could approach $570 billion in 2026. These figures measure different aspects of financing and spending, so you can’t add them together, but they illustrate the extraordinary scale of the financial commitment to developing artificial intelligence.

Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency reported in its 2026 Global Critical Minerals Outlook that global investment in critical minerals actually declined by 9% in 2025, ending several years of growth. The same report noted that public financing commitments in advanced economies had reached approximately $65 billion, more than four times the 2023 level. Even so, this figure reflects commitments rather than actual disbursements, and it covers a broad range of critical mineral projects rather than just the processing and manufacturing capabilities I regard as the most important industrial bottlenecks.

The contrast is striking. Financial markets are prepared to finance a technological revolution whose ultimate commercial structure remains uncertain, but they remain reluctant to finance the industrial infrastructure needed to sustain the physical economy on which that revolution depends.

I am not suggesting that artificial intelligence is unimportant. I believe that it will become an increasingly valuable tool in scientific research, engineering, manufacturing, and business management. My concern is that we are once again confusing the creation of financial wealth with the creation of productive industrial capability.

I have spent more than sixty years working in, managing, researching, and observing industrial manufacturing and the technologies that support it. During that time, I have watched the United States transform from the world’s preeminent industrial manufacturing economy into one increasingly dependent on other nations’ industrial output. This transformation was not inevitable. It was the foreseeable consequence of decisions made by corporate management, investors, financial institutions, and governments. Those decisions were generally justified in the name of economic efficiency, but they too often measured efficiency by returns on financial capital rather than a nation’s long-term productive capacity.

What we now call the critical minerals crisis is, in my opinion, a symptom of a much larger problem: the financial abandonment of American industrial manufacturing.

The International Energy Agency has offered a particularly revealing comparison. In its 2026 study of rare earth supply chains, the agency estimated that developing diversified magnet rare earth supply chains outside the dominant supplier, China, would require about $60 billion in investment over the next decade. Nearly half of this investment would go to refining, while about one-third would go to magnet manufacturing.

Consider what this means. The estimated capital required over ten years to substantially diversify the world’s rare-earth magnet supply chain is less than one-tenth of the annual capital spending now being planned by the largest technology companies.

The comparison isn’t exact because the two figures reflect different industrial activities, geographies, and time periods. But the difference in scale is so enormous that it raises a question about our financial system’s priorities.

Why is it relatively easy to mobilize hundreds of billions of dollars to build data centers, yet so difficult to finance the chemical separation plants, metal production facilities, alloy plants, and magnet factories that underpin the manufacturing of essential electrical and electronic equipment?

The answer is not that the industrial importance of these facilities is uncertain. The IEA estimates that fully implementing China’s expanded rare earth export restrictions could jeopardize as much as $6.5 trillion in annual downstream production outside China. This estimates economic activity exposed to disruption, not a prediction that $6.5 trillion will actually be lost. Nevertheless, it illustrates the extraordinary economic leverage a relatively small number of critical materials and processing capabilities can exert.

We are discussing a potential vulnerability measured in trillions of dollars, whose mitigation may require investments measured in tens of billions.

This is an astonishing imbalance between an industrial capability’s economic importance and financial markets’ willingness to provide the capital needed to establish it.

A rare earth separation plant may be essential to producing thousands of manufactured products, yet it may never offer investors the financial returns expected from a successful artificial intelligence software company. Its value to the national economy may be enormous, while its profitability as an individual enterprise may be relatively modest.

This distinction between industrial importance and financial attractiveness is the central problem that American industrial policy has failed to resolve.

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally an information-processing technology. Its economic value will ultimately depend on its ability to improve productivity, reduce costs, accelerate innovation, or create products and services customers will pay for. These are legitimate objectives, and some applications will undoubtedly become enormously valuable.

But artificial intelligence does not eliminate the physical requirements of industrial civilization.

A computer cannot manufacture an electric motor without copper, steel, insulation, and, in many applications, rare earth permanent magnets. It cannot produce a semiconductor without highly purified and precisely engineered materials. It cannot construct an electrical transmission system without conductors, transformers, and the industrial facilities required to manufacture them. It cannot build a factory without machinery, nor can it replace the chemical engineering, metallurgy, process development, and manufacturing experience required to produce materials consistently at commercial scale.

Artificial intelligence may help engineers design improved chemical separation systems. It may optimize an existing metallurgical plant’s operation. It may help identify process inefficiencies and accelerate materials research. But engineers must still demonstrate the resulting improvements in physical equipment, using actual feedstocks, under conditions that can be reproduced economically in commercial production.

The expansion of artificial intelligence may increase demand for many critical materials whose supply chains are already fragile. Data centers require enormous investments in electrical generation and distribution, cooling equipment, transformers, conductors, and electronic components. Advanced semiconductors require highly specialized materials and extraordinarily sophisticated manufacturing equipment. The physical infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence is not virtual. It is an industrial system.
